statement: Every [regular](c:regular-space) [Lindelöf space](c:lindelof-space) is [normal](c:normal-space). Any two disjoint [closed](c:closed-set) sets have disjoint open neighborhoods.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is [regular](c:regular-space): a point and a closed set that misses it have disjoint open neighborhoods.
The space $X$ is a [Lindelöf space](c:lindelof-space): every open cover has a countable subcover.

conclusion: The space $X$ is [normal](c:normal-space): disjoint closed sets $A$ and $B$ have disjoint open neighborhoods.

formal.difference: The declaration states that two disjoint closed sets of a regular Lindelöf space have a separating cover. This is the key step of the proof, a related and smaller fact.

proofs.name: Countable separating covers
proofs.slogan: Cover each closed set by countably many open sets whose closures miss the other set, then trim the overlaps.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. No $T_1$ or Hausdorff assumption is needed. A regular second countable space is Lindelöf, so it is normal too.

roles.why: Regularity gives, for each point of $A$, an open neighborhood whose closure misses $B$.
The Lindelöf property reduces the cover of the closed set $A$ to a countable one.

steps.slogan: Cover the closed set $A$ by open sets whose closures miss $B$.
steps.detail: Let $A$ and $B$ be disjoint [closed](c:closed-set) sets. For each $a \in A$, regularity gives an open $U_a \ni a$ with $\overline{U_a} \cap B = \emptyset$. These sets and $X \setminus A$ form an [open cover](c:open-cover) of $X$.

steps.slogan: Select countable families of open sets that cover $A$ and $B$.
steps.detail: A countable subcover gives open sets $U_0, U_1, \dots$ with $A \subseteq \bigcup U_n$ and $\overline{U_n} \cap B = \emptyset$; drop $X \setminus A$, which misses $A$. The same argument gives open sets $V_n$ with $B \subseteq \bigcup V_n$ and $\overline{V_n} \cap A = \emptyset$.

steps.slogan: Trim each set by the closures of the earlier sets of the other family.
steps.detail: Put $U'_n = U_n \setminus \bigcup_{k \le n} \overline{V_k}$ and $V'_n = V_n \setminus \bigcup_{k \le n} \overline{U_k}$. A finite union of closed sets is closed, so these sets are open.

steps.slogan: Show that the trimmed unions still contain $A$ and $B$.
steps.detail: Put $U = \bigcup U'_n$ and $V = \bigcup V'_n$. A point $a \in A$ lies in some $U_n$ and in no $\overline{V_k}$, because $\overline{V_k} \cap A = \emptyset$. So $a \in U'_n$. In the same way $B \subseteq V$.

steps.slogan: Show that the open sets $U$ and $V$ are disjoint.
steps.detail: Suppose $x \in U'_n \cap V'_m$. If $n \le m$, then $x \in U_n \subseteq \overline{U_n}$, but $V'_m$ excludes $\overline{U_k}$ for every $k \le m$, including $k = n$. This is a contradiction. If $m \le n$, swap the roles. So $U \cap V = \emptyset$, and $X$ is [normal](c:normal-space).

concepts.c:regular-space: Regularity separates each point of $A$ from $B$ by a closure.
concepts.c:lindelof-space: The Lindelöf property makes the cover of $A$ countable.
concepts.c:normal-space: Normality is the property that the proof builds.
concepts.c:closed-set: The closed sets $A$ and $B$ are the sets to separate, and closures are closed.
concepts.c:open-cover: The cover by the sets $U_a$ and $X \setminus A$ is the input to the Lindelöf property.

statement: Let $X$ be a separable [complete metric space](c:complete-metric-space) with metric $d$. Let $U \neq X$ be open, $\delta(x) = \inf\{d(x,z) : z \notin U\}$, and $d'(x,y) = d(x,y) + |1/\delta(x) - 1/\delta(y)|$ on $U$. Then $d'$ is a metric that induces the subspace topology, and $(U, d')$ is complete. So $U$ is [Polish](c:polish-space).

hypotheses.text: The set $U \neq X$ is open, so its complement is closed and nonempty.

conclusion: The function $d'$ is a complete metric on $U$ that induces the subspace topology, so $U$ is separable and completely metrizable.

proofs.name: Metric that blows up at the boundary
proofs.slogan: Add the term $|1/\delta(x) - 1/\delta(y)|$ to the metric, so Cauchy sequences stay away from the boundary.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for $U \neq X$; for $U = X$ there is nothing to prove. The old metric $d$ on $U$ is not complete in general.

roles.why: The condition $x \in U$ gives $\delta(x) > 0$, so $d'$ is finite, and the complement of $U$ is closed.
Completeness of $X$ gives a limit point of a $d'$-Cauchy sequence.
Separability of $X$ passes to the subspace $U$.

steps.slogan: Check that $d'$ is a metric on $U$.
steps.detail: For $x, y \in U$ we have $\delta(x) > 0$, so $d'$ is finite and symmetric. The triangle inequality holds because $d$ and $(x,y) \mapsto |1/\delta(x) - 1/\delta(y)|$ both satisfy it. If $d'(x,y) = 0$, then $d(x,y) = 0$, so $x = y$.

steps.slogan: Show that $d$ and $d'$ induce the same topology on $U$.
steps.detail: Since $d \le d'$, every $d'$-ball lies in the $d$-ball of the same radius, so every $d$-open set is $d'$-open. Conversely fix $x \in U$ and $\varepsilon > 0$. The map $y \mapsto 1/\delta(y)$ is continuous at $x$, so a small $r$ gives $d(x,y) < \varepsilon/2$ and $|1/\delta(x) - 1/\delta(y)| < \varepsilon/2$ for $d(x,y) < r$. Then $d'(x,y) < \varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Bound a $d'$-Cauchy sequence away from the boundary.
steps.detail: Let $(x_n)$ be $d'$-Cauchy in $U$. Since $d \le d'$, it is $d$-Cauchy, so it converges to some $x \in X$ by completeness. The sequence $(1/\delta(x_n))$ is Cauchy in $\mathbb{R}$, because $|1/\delta(x_n) - 1/\delta(x_m)| \le d'(x_n, x_m)$. So it is bounded by some $C > 0$, and $\delta(x_n) \ge 1/C$.

steps.slogan: Show that the limit lies in $U$ and is a $d'$-limit.
steps.detail: The function $\delta$ is continuous on $X$, so $\delta(x) = \lim \delta(x_n) \ge 1/C > 0$. The complement of $U$ is closed, so $\delta(x) > 0$ gives $x \in U$. By the topology step, $x_n \to x$ in $d$ gives $d'(x_n, x) \to 0$. So $(U, d')$ is complete.

steps.slogan: Pass separability to $U$ and conclude that $U$ is Polish.
steps.detail: A countable base of $X$ restricts to a countable base of $U$, and one point from each nonempty member gives a countable dense subset. The topology of $U$ is the same for $d$ and $d'$, so $U$ is separable and completely metrizable.

concepts.c:complete-metric-space: Completeness of $X$ gives the limit of the Cauchy sequence.
concepts.c:separable-metric-space: Separability of $X$ gives a countable dense subset of $U$.
concepts.c:polish-space: The proof shows that $U$ is separable and completely metrizable.

statement: Let $E$ be a real [inner product space](c:inner-product-space), $v$ a unit vector, $H = v^\perp$ and $S$ the unit [sphere](c:sphere). Then $\sigma_v(x) = 2(x - \langle x,v\rangle v)/(1 - \langle x,v\rangle)$ is a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) from $S \setminus \{v\}$ onto $H$, with inverse $\tau_v(w) = ((|w|^2-4)v + 4w)/(|w|^2+4)$. The transition map from $\sigma_v$ to $\sigma_{-v}$ is $w \mapsto 4w/|w|^2$.

hypotheses.text: The space $E$ is a real [inner product space](c:inner-product-space).
The vector $v$ is a unit vector and $H$ is its orthogonal complement.

conclusion: The map $\sigma_v$ is a homeomorphism with inverse $\tau_v$, the transition map on $H \setminus \{0\}$ is $w \mapsto 4w/|w|^2$, and the two charts form a smooth [atlas](c:atlas) of $S$.

formal.difference: The declaration states one half of the statement: the inverse map composed with the projection is the identity on the sphere minus $v$. It does not state the transition map.

proofs.name: Direct computation
proofs.slogan: Check by computation that $\tau_v$ and $\sigma_v$ are inverse maps, then compute the transition map.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for any dimension of $E$. The smooth atlas claim for finite dimension $n+1$ shows that $S$ is a smooth $n$-manifold.

roles.why: The inner product gives the formulas, the Pythagorean identity and continuity.
The unit vector $v$ makes $H$ a complement of $v$ and gives $|\tau_v(w)|^2 = 1$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\tau_v$ maps $H$ into $S \setminus \{v\}$.
Show that $\sigma_v \circ \tau_v$ is the identity on $H$.
steps.detail: We have $\langle \tau_v(w), v\rangle = t$ and $1 - t = 8/(|w|^2+4)$. The $H$-component of $\tau_v(w)$ is $uw$. So $\sigma_v(\tau_v(w)) = 2uw/(1-t) = w$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\tau_v \circ \sigma_v$ is the identity on $S \setminus \{v\}$.
steps.detail: Let $x \in S \setminus \{v\}$, $a = \langle x, v\rangle < 1$ and $w = \sigma_v(x)$. Since $|x| = 1$, $|x - av|^2 = 1 - a^2$, so $|w|^2 = 4(1+a)/(1-a)$. Then $t = a$ and $u = (1-a)/2$, so $\tau_v(w) = av + (x - av) = x$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $\sigma_v$ is a homeomorphism onto $H$.
steps.detail: Both maps are given by formulas that use inner products, norms, sums and quotients. Their denominators $1 - \langle x,v\rangle > 0$ and $|w|^2+4 > 0$ never vanish. So both maps are continuous and inverse, and $\sigma_v$ is a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism).

steps.slogan: Compute the transition map to the chart at $-v$.
steps.detail: The overlap is $S \setminus \{v,-v\}$, which $\sigma_v$ maps onto $H \setminus \{0\}$ because $\tau_v(0) = -v$. For $x = \tau_v(w)$ with $w \neq 0$, we have $a = t$ and $1 + t = 2|w|^2/(|w|^2+4)$. The $H$-component of $x$ is $4w/(|w|^2+4)$. So $\sigma_{-v}(x) = 2 \cdot (4w/(|w|^2+4)) / (1+t) = 4w/|w|^2$.

steps.slogan: Show that the two charts form a smooth [atlas](c:atlas).
steps.detail: The map $w \mapsto 4w/|w|^2$ is smooth on $H \setminus \{0\}$ and is its own inverse. So both transition maps are smooth, and the charts $\sigma_v$ and $\sigma_{-v}$, which cover $S$, form a smooth atlas.

concepts.c:inner-product-space: The inner product defines $\sigma_v$, $H$ and the norms in the computation.
concepts.c:sphere: The sphere is the space that the two charts cover.
concepts.c:homeomorphism: The two inverse continuous maps make $\sigma_v$ a homeomorphism.
concepts.c:atlas: Two charts with smooth transition maps form a smooth atlas.

statement: Let $X$, $Y$, $Z$ be topological spaces and give $C(Y,Z)$ the [compact-open topology](c:compact-open-topology). (a) If $F\colon X \times Y \to Z$ is continuous, then $x \mapsto F(x,\cdot)$ is continuous. (b) If $Y$ is [locally compact](c:locally-compact-space) and $f\colon X \to C(Y,Z)$ is continuous, then $(x,y) \mapsto f(x)(y)$ is continuous.

hypotheses.text: The sets $X$, $Y$, $Z$ are topological spaces, and $C(Y,Z)$ has the [compact-open topology](c:compact-open-topology).
For part (b), the space $Y$ is [locally compact](c:locally-compact-space): every point has a compact neighborhood inside each of its neighborhoods.

conclusion: For locally compact $Y$, continuous maps $X \times Y \to Z$ correspond to continuous maps $X \to C(Y,Z)$ by [currying](c:currying).

formal.difference: The declaration states part (a) only: a jointly continuous map curries to a continuous map into the function space. It does not state part (b).

proofs.name: Tube lemma and evaluation map
proofs.slogan: Prove part (a) with the tube lemma, and part (b) by the continuity of the evaluation map.
proofs.scope: Both parts. Part (a) needs no assumption on the spaces. The proof gives a bijection of sets of continuous maps, not a homeomorphism of function spaces.

roles.why: The sets $V(K,U)$ generate the topology of $C(Y,Z)$, and part (a) holds for all spaces.
A compact neighborhood $K$ of $y_0$ inside $g_0^{-1}(U)$ makes the evaluation map continuous.

steps.slogan: Reduce continuity of $f$ to preimages of subbasic sets $V(K,U)$.
steps.detail: The topology of $C(Y,Z)$ is generated by the sets $V(K,U)$ of maps that send the compact set $K$ into the open set $U$. So $f$ is continuous if each $f^{-1}(V(K,U))$ is open.

steps.slogan: Prove part (a) with the tube lemma.
steps.detail: Let $f(x) = F(x,\cdot)$. Then $f^{-1}(V(K,U)) = \{x : F(\{x\} \times K) \subseteq U\}$. Let $x_0$ be in it. The open set $W = F^{-1}(U)$ contains $\{x_0\} \times K$. The tube lemma gives an open $A \ni x_0$ with $A \times K \subseteq W$, so $A \subseteq f^{-1}(V(K,U))$.

steps.slogan: Choose a compact neighborhood for part (b).
steps.detail: Let $(g_0, y_0) \in C(Y,Z) \times Y$ and let $U$ be open with $g_0(y_0) \in U$. Then $g_0^{-1}(U)$ is an open neighborhood of $y_0$. Local compactness gives a compact $K$ with $y_0 \in \operatorname{int} K$ and $K \subseteq g_0^{-1}(U)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the evaluation map is continuous.
steps.detail: The set $V(K,U) \times \operatorname{int} K$ is an open neighborhood of $(g_0, y_0)$. For $(g,y)$ in it, $g(y) \in g(K) \subseteq U$. So the [evaluation map](c:evaluation-map) $(g,y) \mapsto g(y)$ is continuous at $(g_0, y_0)$.

steps.slogan: Write the uncurried map as a composite of continuous maps.
steps.detail: We have $F(x,y) = f(x)(y) = \mathrm{ev}(f(x), y) = (\mathrm{ev} \circ (f \times \mathrm{id}))(x,y)$. The map $f \times \mathrm{id}$ and the evaluation map are continuous, so $F$ is continuous. This proves part (b).

steps.slogan: Join the two parts into a correspondence of continuous maps.
steps.detail: Currying and uncurrying are inverse bijections between all maps $X \times Y \to Z$ and all maps $X \to C(Y,Z)$. Part (a) shows that currying keeps continuity, and part (b) shows that uncurrying keeps it when $Y$ is locally compact.

concepts.c:compact-open-topology: Its subbasic sets $V(K,U)$ are the sets whose preimages the proof studies.
concepts.c:locally-compact-space: Local compactness supplies the compact neighborhood $K$.
concepts.c:currying: Currying is the correspondence that the theorem proves.
concepts.c:evaluation-map: Its continuity turns a continuous $f$ into a continuous $F$.

statement: Let $f$ be a [convex function](c:convex-function) on an interval $I$. Let $x_1 \ge \dots \ge x_n$ and $y_1 \ge \dots \ge y_n$ lie in $I$, with $\sum_{i \le k} x_i \le \sum_{i \le k} y_i$ for $k < n$ and equal total sums. Then $\sum f(x_i) \le \sum f(y_i)$. If $f$ is strictly convex, equality holds only if $x_i = y_i$ for all $i$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is a [convex function](c:convex-function) on the interval $I$; the endpoints may belong to $I$.
Both lists are sorted in decreasing order and lie in $I$.
The partial sums satisfy $\sum_{i \le k} x_i \le \sum_{i \le k} y_i$ for $k = 1, \dots, n-1$.
For the equality case, $f$ is strictly convex.

conclusion: The inequality $\sum f(x_i) \le \sum f(y_i)$ holds, and for strictly convex $f$ equality implies $x = y$.

formal.difference: The declaration states a related and smaller fact: the slopes of a convex function increase over three ordered points. It is the only convexity fact that the proof uses.

proofs.name: Chord slopes and Abel summation
proofs.slogan: Write the difference of the two sums with chord slopes, then sum by parts against the partial sums.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The entropy corollary follows with $f(t) = t \ln t$: a probability vector majorized by another has the larger Shannon entropy.

roles.why: Convexity makes the chord slopes $c_i$ monotone.
The order of the lists gives the moves $x_{i+1} \le x_i$ and $y_{i+1} \le y_i$ in the slope comparison.
It gives $D_k \ge 0$, so each summand is nonnegative.
It gives $D_n = 0$, which removes the last term of the Abel sum.
Strict convexity makes the slope inequalities strict.

steps.slogan: Delete the indices with $x_i = y_i$.
steps.detail: Each deleted pair adds $0$ to every partial difference, and it removes the same value $f(x_i) = f(y_i)$ from both sides. The remaining lists are still sorted. So assume $x_i \neq y_i$ for all $i$.

steps.slogan: Show that the chord slope is monotone in each argument.
steps.detail: Let $s(a,b) = (f(b) - f(a))/(b - a)$. For $a < b < c$ in $I$, convexity gives $s(a,b) \le s(a,c) \le s(b,c)$. Fix $v$. In each of the three orders of $u < u'$ and $v$, these inequalities give $s(u,v) \le s(u',v)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the slopes $c_i = s(x_i, y_i)$ decrease with $i$.
steps.detail: If $x_{i+1} \neq y_i$, then $c_i \ge s(x_{i+1}, y_i) \ge s(x_{i+1}, y_{i+1})$: move the first argument down, then the second. If $x_{i+1} = y_i$, then $x_i \neq y_{i+1}$, and the other route $c_i \ge s(x_i, y_{i+1}) \ge s(x_{i+1}, y_{i+1})$ works.

steps.slogan: Sum by parts with the partial differences $D_k$.
steps.detail: Put $d_i = y_i - x_i$ and $D_k = d_1 + \dots + d_k$. Then $f(y_i) - f(x_i) = c_i d_i$, so [Abel summation](c:abel-summation) gives $\sum (f(y_i) - f(x_i)) = \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} (c_k - c_{k+1}) D_k + c_n D_n$. The term with $D_n = 0$ vanishes.

steps.slogan: Show that every summand is nonnegative.
steps.detail: Each $c_k - c_{k+1} \ge 0$ and each $D_k \ge 0$. So the sum is nonnegative, and $\sum f(x_i) \le \sum f(y_i)$.

steps.slogan: Show that strict convexity forces $x = y$ in the equality case.
steps.detail: Suppose some index remains after the deletion. Then $D_1 = y_1 - x_1 > 0$, and $n \ge 2$. For strictly convex $f$, $c_k = c_{k+1}$ forces $x_k = x_{k+1}$ and $y_k = y_{k+1}$, so $d_{k+1} = d_k$. If every $k$ with $D_k > 0$ had $c_k = c_{k+1}$, then $d_k = d_1$ for all $k$ and $D_n = n d_1 > 0$, which is false. So the sum is positive, and equality needs $x_i = y_i$ for all $i$.

concepts.c:convex-function: Convexity gives the monotone chord slopes.
concepts.c:abel-summation: Summation by parts turns the slope sum into a sum against $D_k$.

statement: Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ Hermitian [positive semidefinite matrix](c:positive-semidefinite-matrix). Then $\det A \le a_{11} \cdots a_{nn}$, and for positive definite $A$ equality holds only if $A$ is diagonal. For a complex square matrix $M$ with columns $m_j$, $|\det M| \le \prod \|m_j\|$. So $|\det M| \le n^{n/2}$ if all entries are $\pm 1$.

hypotheses.text: The matrix $A$ is Hermitian and [positive semidefinite](c:positive-semidefinite-matrix): $x^*Ax \ge 0$ for all $x$.
The norm $\|\cdot\|$ is the Euclidean norm.
For the equality case, $A$ is positive definite.

conclusion: The bound $\det A \le \prod a_{ii}$ holds with the stated equality case. Also $|\det M| \le \prod \|m_j\|$, with equality for $\det M \neq 0$ only when the columns are orthogonal, and $|\det M| \le n^{n/2}$ for $\pm 1$ entries.

formal.difference: The declaration states a related and smaller fact: the determinant of a positive semidefinite matrix is nonnegative. The proof uses it for $\det B \ge 0$. It does not state the Hadamard inequality.

proofs.name: Normalize the diagonal and use the mean inequality
proofs.slogan: Scale the matrix to a unit diagonal, then bound its determinant by the mean of its eigenvalues.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The equality statement for singular $A$ is only partial: equality can also hold when a diagonal entry is zero. The row version follows by transposing.

roles.why: It gives $a_{ii} \ge 0$, the scaled matrix $B$ and its nonnegative real eigenvalues.
It makes $a_{jj} = \|m_j\|^2$ for $A = M^*M$ and gives the norm $\sqrt{n}$ of a $\pm 1$ column.
It makes all eigenvalues of $B$ positive, so the equality case of the mean inequality applies.

steps.slogan: Treat the case of a zero diagonal entry.
steps.detail: Suppose $a_{ii} = 0$. For real $t$, $x = te_i + e_j$ gives $x^*Ax = 2t\,\mathrm{Re}\,a_{ij} + a_{jj} \ge 0$ for both signs of $t$, so $\mathrm{Re}\,a_{ij} = 0$; the same holds for $\mathrm{Im}\,a_{ij}$. So row $i$ is zero, $\det A = 0$, and the bound is an equality. Assume now $a_{ii} > 0$.

steps.slogan: Scale $A$ to a matrix $B$ with unit diagonal.
steps.detail: Let $D = \mathrm{diag}(a_{11}^{-1/2}, \dots, a_{nn}^{-1/2})$ and $B = DAD$. Then $B$ is positive semidefinite with $b_{ii} = 1$, and $\det B = \det A/(a_{11} \cdots a_{nn})$.

steps.slogan: Bound $\det B$ by the mean of the eigenvalues of $B$.
steps.detail: The Hermitian matrix $B$ has real [eigenvalues](c:eigenvalue) $\mu_i \ge 0$ with [determinant](c:determinant) $\det B = \prod \mu_i$ and [trace](c:trace-of-a-matrix) $\sum \mu_i = n$. The AM-GM inequality gives $\det B \le (\sum \mu_i / n)^n = 1$. So $\det A \le \prod a_{ii}$.

steps.slogan: Find the equality case for positive definite $A$.
steps.detail: If $\det A = \prod a_{ii}$, then $\prod \mu_i = (\sum \mu_i / n)^n$ with all $\mu_i > 0$. The equality case of AM-GM gives $\mu_i = 1$ for all $i$, so the Hermitian $B$ is the identity and $A = D^{-1}D^{-1}$ is diagonal. A diagonal $A$ gives equality.

steps.slogan: Apply the bound to $A = M^*M$ for a general matrix $M$.
steps.detail: The matrix $A$ is positive semidefinite with $\det A = |\det M|^2$ and $a_{jj} = \|m_j\|^2$. So $|\det M| \le \prod \|m_j\|$. If $\det M \neq 0$, then $A$ is positive definite, and equality holds exactly when $M^*M$ is diagonal, that is, when the columns are orthogonal.

steps.slogan: Bound the determinant of a matrix with entries $\pm 1$.
steps.detail: Every column of such an $n \times n$ matrix has norm $\sqrt{n}$. So $|\det M| \le (\sqrt{n})^n = n^{n/2}$.

concepts.c:positive-semidefinite-matrix: Positive semidefiniteness gives the real nonnegative eigenvalues of $B$.
concepts.c:determinant: The determinant is the product of the eigenvalues that the proof bounds.
concepts.c:eigenvalue: The eigenvalues of $B$ have product $\det B$ and sum $n$.
concepts.c:trace-of-a-matrix: The trace of $B$ equals $n$ because the diagonal is all ones.
